contexts.context: Tekeste et al. (2018) developed a DEM model for one material—combine-harvested corn—using 27 Latin-hypercube simulations across four particle-interaction parameters and four shape approximations (1, 2, 5, 13 spheres). Calibration fitted bucket- and anchor-lifted angle of repose (AOR) via regression/meta-models; the 2-sphere model performed best (bucket AOR \(R^2=0.9423\), anchor \(R^2=0.5412\)). Auger flow rate and static AOR were held out for validation, with errors of 2.8–9.6% and 1.26–8.55%. No Bayesian uncertainty quantification, multi-powder study, or independent standard-test validation was reported.

contexts.context: Haeri (2017) uses device-scale DEM to optimize blade-spreader geometry for powder-bed fusion, targeting minimum bed void fraction. Simulations initially use simple rod-shaped grains to reduce computational cost; blade profiles are parameterized by three super-ellipse dimensions. The study then develops a multi-sphere approximation for realistic 3D grain shapes and shows the optimized blade can achieve bed quality comparable to or better than a counter-rotating roller. It discusses particle size, morphology, angle of repose, flowability, and packing fraction, but the excerpt reports no auger/screw dosing data, Bayesian or uncertainty-based parameter inference, multi-powder calibration, or validation against independent standard tests.

contexts.context: A 2025 study developed Bayesian-optimization DEM calibration for metallic PBF-LM powders, minimizing squared error between experimentally measured and simulated consolidation void ratios. It examined cohesion, stiffness, and stress scaling, including matched “σ/E” to permit lower DEM stiffness and larger time steps. Simulations used stresses from 0.225 to 9000 Pa; at 9 kPa, excessive compression lowered simulated void ratio. The authors found consolidation is dominated by normal forces, whereas spreading is governed by tangential sliding and shear. Parameters calibrated for consolidation did not reproduce spreading, motivating phenomenon-specific, multi-stage calibration and validation.

contexts.context: This excerpt identifies Imole et al. (2016; originally submitted 2014) as a relevant non-El-Kassem study involving experimental screw-feeder dosing and DEM calibration. The authors use a simplified canister box with a constant-pitch screw feeder, applying discrete rotation steps followed by rest periods. They vary dosage time, coil pitch, and initial powder mass, and report that dosed mass increases approximately linearly with dosage time and rotation speed, whereas changing the number of coils does not produce a directly proportional change in output. Crucially, the DEM model calibrates interparticle friction and cohesion against the dosing experiments and then reproduces the experimental findings quantitatively, although the excerpt notes limitations: simulations involve smaller masses and overestimate arching and blockage. The paper also frames particle scaling and adaptation of particle properties as methods for simulating fine cohesive powders. However, these pages provide no evidence of Bayesian calibration, Bayesian optimization, posterior inference, multiple-powder comparison, or held-out validation using shear, Hall/Carney flowability, tapped density, spreading, tapping, tilt, fill level, afterflow, or intermittency responses. Thus, it is evidence for throughput-based friction/cohesion calibration and for testing blockage-related behavior, but not for the broader multi-regime or Bayesian workflows requested.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes El Kassem et al. (2021), a semi-automated DEM calibration method for pharmaceutical powders using a vertical auger dosing setup. It is directly relevant as a baseline for comparing other screw-feeder calibration studies, but it is itself an El-Kassem work and therefore does not satisfy the request for independent non-El-Kassem literature. The method extracts three measured bulk responses from auger experiments—angle of repose, bulk density, and mass flow rate—and uses Design of Experiments (DoE) and multivariate regression analysis (MVRA) to relate responses to DEM parameters. The varied factors include auger speed, particle-particle and particle-wall static friction, and particle-particle rolling friction. Predicted behaviors across all three responses are clustered to reduce parameter non-uniqueness, after which a parameter set is selected that matches experimental reference data. The introduction also notes prior DEM studies involving screw-feeder mass flow rate, screw power, and particle-transfer velocity, and prior DoE calibration of angle of repose and porosity. However, the provided pages contain no evidence of Bayesian posterior inference, Bayesian optimization, calibration across several powders, held-out shear/Hall/Carney/tapped-density/spreading validation, or fitting of tapping, tilt, fill-level, afterflow, or intermittency responses. Shen (2021), Katagiri (2025), and powder-spreadability studies are not present in this excerpt.

contexts.context: This excerpt documents El Kassem et al. (2021) as a DEM calibration study using an auger dosing machine, rather than merely using a feeder for validation. The method jointly calibrates particle–particle and particle–wall static friction and particle–particle rolling friction against three measured bulk responses: angle of repose (AoR), mass flow rate (ṁ), and bulk density (BD), evaluated as functions of auger speed. A D-optimal design, multivariate regression response models, superimposed contour plots, and optimization were used to reduce parameter non-uniqueness. The authors emphasize that individual calibration tests leave substantial ambiguity because many DEM parameter combinations produce similar bulk behavior. Their selected parameter combination was experimentally validated, with a maximum deviation of 2.86% and an overall mean deviation of 0.87% across 12 responses; they report achieving comparable accuracy with 20 simulations rather than 384. The excerpt does not provide evidence about other non-El-Kassem works, Shen (2021), Katagiri (2025), Bayesian posterior calibration, Bayesian optimization, multiple powders, held-out shear/Hall/Carney/tapped-density/spreading tests, or fitting tapping, tilt, fill-level, afterflow, or intermittency responses. Its relevance is methodological and comparative: Karkala et al. calibrate cohesive DEM parameters using measured dynamic yield strength and shear-cell responses rather than feeder throughput. Their JKR-based framework treats surface energy as highly influential in dynamic-yield-strength simulations, while sliding and rolling friction also affect the result. Because shear-cell critical-state shear remains sensitive to surface energy, the authors combine DYS and shear-cell simulations to identify friction parameters and calibrated cohesion. The study reports successful calibration for experimentally sized and scaled particles, altered shear modulus, and alternate friction sets, with simulated DYS values within 5% of experiment. The excerpt also emphasizes that DEM calibration is difficult and notes prior noncohesive calibration using sandpiles, angle of repose, hourglass discharge, and shear cells. Thus, it can serve as a baseline for distinguishing conventional response matching with prescribed friction/cohesion from Bayesian calibration or Bayesian optimization based on screw throughput and multiple held-out responses such as shear, Hall flow, tapped density, spreading, tapping, tilt, fill level, afterflow, or intermittency. contexts.context: El Kassem et al. establish a DEM calibration method for one free-flowing/non-cohesive powder using an auger doser and three jointly fitted bulk responses: angle of repose (AoR), bulk density (BD), and mass flow rate (ṁ), related to particle–particle/wall static friction and rolling friction. A D-optimal design and multivariate regression used only 20 simulations (versus 384 previously); validation across 12 results had 0.87% mean and 2.86% maximum deviation. They emphasize ambiguity from single tests, identify rolling friction as dominant, and recommend future work on more properties and cohesive powders.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. El Kassem et al. (KONA Powder and Particle Journal 38, 2021, 235-250, doi:10.14356/kona.2021010) calibrated DEM contact parameters of one free-flowing lactose powder from the angle of repose, bulk density and mass flow rate measured with an auger dosing device, using a design of experiments and regression. Beyond that paper and its direct predecessors by the same group: has anyone used the measured response of a screw or auger doser or feeder (mass per revolution or flow rate versus screw speed, tilt angle or fill level, flow intermittency, afterflow) as the primary data to infer DEM or continuum contact parameters for several different powders, with uncertainty quantification such as Bayesian calibration, and then checked the inferred values against standard tests that were not used in the fit (shear cell, Hall or Carney flow, tapped density, spreading)?

contexts.context: Imole et al. (2014) studied a simplified constant-pitch screw feeder for cohesive powders using experiments and DEM. Each dose comprised a rotation step plus rest. They varied dosage time, screw/coil pitch, and initial powder mass, finding dosed mass increased linearly with dosage time and rotation speed, whereas output was not proportional to coil count. They calibrated interparticle friction and cohesion so DEM quantitatively reproduced measurements, but simulations overestimated arching/blockage, especially for smaller masses. The work concerns process-performance calibration, not Bayesian uncertainty quantification, multiple powders, or validation against independent standard tests.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a DEM auger-dosing model using Luding’s linear hysteretic adhesive/plastic contact law, with parameters for stiffness, cohesion, friction, rolling friction, viscosity, and wall friction. Because real powder contains “several billions” of particles, simulations coarse-grain them: experiments use mean diameter 0.184 mm and >10¹⁰ particles, whereas DEM uses 2.50-mm mesoparticles and 3,360 particles for 48 g. Particles settle for 2 s; cohesion is initially reduced to \(k_c/k=0.3\) to prevent packing inhomogeneity and arching, then activated. Cohesion \(k_c/k=0.873\) and friction \(\mu=0.5\)–0.65 are varied.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Cheng et al. (2019) conditioning the DEM calibration on experimental stress–strain curves from cyclic oedometric compression of glass beads. The DEM packing was initialized using a particle configuration obtained from 3D feature-based image processing of 3DXRCT images. During filtering, the model returned macroscopic porosity, stress, and strain along the cyclic loading path; unloading–reloading cycles were especially informative for reducing micromechanical parameter uncertainty. The posterior concerned contact-level DEM parameters, particularly Young’s modulus Ec, interparticle friction µ, and rolling parameters km and ηm. answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. El Kassem et al. (KONA Powder and Particle Journal 38, 2021, 235-250, doi:10.14356/kona.2021010) calibrated DEM contact parameters of one free-flowing lactose powder from the angle of repose, bulk density and mass flow rate measured with an auger dosing device, using a design of experiments and regression. Beyond that paper and its direct predecessors by the same group: has anyone used the measured response of a screw or auger doser or feeder (mass per revolution or flow rate versus screw speed, tilt angle or fill level, flow intermittency, afterflow) as the primary data to infer DEM or continuum contact parameters for several different powders, with uncertainty quantification such as Bayesian calibration, and then checked the inferred values against standard tests that were not used in the fit (shear cell, Hall or Carney flow, tapped density, spreading)?

No. ## Literature assessment

**I found no study that demonstrates the complete workflow described:** infer DEM or continuum contact parameters *primarily from screw/auger dosing responses for several distinct powders*, quantify parameter uncertainty with Bayesian calibration, and then test predictions against previously unused shear, funnel-flow, density, and powder-spreading measurements. This is a conclusion about the literature located and examined, not proof that no such study exists. Crucially, however, **doser-output-based contact-parameter calibration itself is not new**: two independent precedents beyond El Kassem and colleagues directly fit DEM parameters to measured screw-dosing output. (imole2016reprintof"experiments pages 1-5, imole2016reprintof"experiments pages 34-37, shen2021calibrationofdiscrete pages 1-2, shen2021calibrationofdiscrete pages 8-10)

The distinction is which measurements determine the parameters and which provide genuinely independent tests:

| Study | Calibration observations and material(s) | Independent check or consequence | Why it is not an exact match |
|---|---|---|---|
| Imole et al. (2016) | **Cocoa powder:** fitted interparticle friction and cohesion to experimental mass per dose from a screw doser. (imole2016reprintof"experiments pages 1-5, imole2016reprintof"experiments pages 34-37, imole2016reprintof"experiments media 1771b355) | Examined dose duration, screw speed, pitch/coil count, initial mass, arching, and blockage; no standardized powder tests. (imole2016reprintof"experiments pages 1-5, imole2016reprintof"experiments pages 5-11) | One powder; deterministic calibration; no Bayesian UQ, held-out shear/Hall/Carney/tap-density tests, or spreading validation. |
| Shen et al. (2021) | **Wheat flour:** fitted JKR surface energy and powder–powder/powder–steel static friction directly to screw-conveyor mass flow. (shen2021calibrationofdiscrete pages 1-2, shen2021calibrationofdiscrete pages 5-7, shen2021calibrationofdiscrete pages 7-8) | Checked flow at 60–140 rpm; reported errors within 3%. (shen2021calibrationofdiscrete pages 8-10) | One powder and one main response; response-surface optimization rather than Bayesian posterior inference; no independent standardized tests or spreading. |
| El Kassem et al. (2021) | **One free-flowing pharmaceutical powder:** jointly matched auger mass flow, bulk density, and angle of repose using DoE/regression. (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 1-2, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 12-13) | Additional auger-speed checks at 400, 600, and 800 rpm; mean deviation across 12 responses was 0.87%. (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 12-13) | One powder; no Bayesian UQ; validation remained within the same auger-derived response family rather than held-out standard tests or spreading. |
| Tekeste et al. (2018) | **Corn:** fitted four friction parameters to bucket-discharge and anchor-lift angle-of-repose tests—not to auger output. (tekeste2018discreteelementmodel pages 1-3, tekeste2018discreteelementmodel pages 8-9) | Commercial-auger mass flow and discharged-pile angle were held-out validations, with reported relative errors of 2.8–9.6% and 1.26–8.55%, respectively. (tekeste2018discreteelementmodel pages 1-3) | Reverse direction from the proposed workflow: conventional tests calibrated the DEM and auger behavior validated it; one granular material and no Bayesian UQ. |
| Gómez et al. (2024) | **Lactose-based powder and paracetamol:** DEM parameters were fitted using FT4 flow-energy and rotating-drum flow-angle responses. (gomez2024investigatingscrewagitatorspeed pages 6-7) | Feeder emptying, mass flow/feed factor, tracer motion, and accumulation patterns served as validation/application cases. (gomez2024investigatingscrewagitatorspeed pages 3-4, gomez2024investigatingscrewagitatorspeed pages 7-8) | Multiple powders, but feeder data were not the primary inverse-calibration data; no posterior uncertainty or held-out AM spreading. |
| Cheng et al. (2019) | **Glass beads:** Bayesian filtering inferred posterior distributions for contact Young’s modulus, sliding friction, rolling stiffness, and rolling friction from cyclic oedometric stress–strain data. (cheng2019aniterativebayesian pages 2-5, cheng2019aniterativebayesian pages 1-2) | Quantified parameter correlations and uncertainty; posterior expectations converged within four iterations. (cheng2019aniterativebayesian pages 1-2, cheng2019aniterativebayesian pages 24-26) | Genuine Bayesian DEM calibration, but no screw/auger response, multiple powders, standard-test cross-validation, or spreading prediction. |
| Katagiri et al. (2025) | **Hastelloy X:** Bayesian optimization selected JKR surface energy and rolling resistance by minimizing consolidation void-ratio error. (katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 1-2, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 2-4) | Transfer to powder spreading produced excessively cohesive, nonuniform beds, exposing a normal-loading versus shear-regime mismatch. (katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 11-14, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 1-2) | Bayesian optimization does not provide the requested parameter posterior/UQ; calibration used consolidation rather than feeder data, and transfer to spreading failed. |


*Table: Comparison of feeder-based DEM calibration studies and adjacent Bayesian or powder-spreading work. The matrix distinguishes calibration data from validation data and shows why none implements the complete proposed workflow.*

**Closest feeder-first precedents.** Imole *et al.* (2016, *Powder Technology*, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2015.07.052) measured cocoa-powder mass per screw dose and calibrated interparticle cohesion and friction against it; their published calibration plot places experimental mass per dose directly against simulated responses over those contact parameters. They also investigated screw speed, dose duration, pitch and initial powder mass, and observed arching/blockage. This is particularly close to a dosing fingerprint, but concerns one powder, does not report Bayesian posteriors, and does not establish agreement with held-out standardized flow tests or recoating. (imole2016reprintof"experiments pages 1-5, imole2016reprintof"experiments pages 5-11, imole2016reprintof"experiments pages 34-37, imole2016reprintof"experiments media 1771b355)

Shen, Li and Xu (2021, *Journal of Engineering*, doi:10.1155/2021/6671511) **explicitly calibrated directly to wheat-flour screw-conveyor mass flow**, using experimental-design screening and response-surface optimization to select JKR surface energy and flour–flour and flour–steel static-friction coefficients. The fitted-flow comparison differed by 1.37%; comparisons at other screw speeds, 60–140 rpm, differed by less than 3%. Those are valuable operating-condition checks, not independent shear-cell, Hall/Carney, tapped-density or spreading validations; the study treats one powder and reports an optimum rather than a Bayesian parameter posterior. (shen2021calibrationofdiscrete pages 1-2, shen2021calibrationofdiscrete pages 5-7, shen2021calibrationofdiscrete pages 8-10)

**Why other apparently close studies do not answer the question.** El Kassem *et al.* fitted auger-derived angle of repose, bulk density and flow rate for a free-flowing material using design of experiments and regression; their additional 400–800-rpm checks remained within the auger-response family. In the opposite calibration direction, Tekeste *et al.* (2018) fitted corn friction parameters to two *angle-of-repose* experiments, then used commercial-auger flow as validation. Gómez *et al.* (2024) used FT4 flow-energy and rotating-drum responses to calibrate powder DEM models, then tested lactose-based and paracetamol feeder behavior. Thus, multiple materials appearing in a feeder paper does not mean multiple materials were **inferred from feeder data**. (kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 1-2, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 12-13, tekeste2018discreteelementmodel pages 1-3, tekeste2018discreteelementmodel pages 8-9, gomez2024investigatingscrewagitatorspeed pages 6-7)

**Bayesian inference and spreading have been demonstrated separately, not in that combination.** Cheng *et al.* (2019, doi:10.1016/j.cma.2019.01.027) inferred distributions and correlations of DEM stiffness and friction parameters using cyclic-compression stress–strain measurements, **not dosing data**. Katagiri *et al.* (2025, doi:10.3390/jmmp9120383) used *Bayesian optimization* to select cohesion and rolling-resistance parameters from metal-powder consolidation void ratio; this optimizes an objective rather than reporting the requested posterior over contact parameters. Applying that parameter set to spreading produced excessively cohesive, nonuniform beds, illustrating that a fit in one deformation regime need not transfer to another. Independent multi-powder studies measure actual recoating quality—for example, Brocksieper *et al.* (2026) tested three metal powders—but do not infer their contacts from screw-doser output. (cheng2019aniterativebayesian pages 1-2, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 2-4, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 1-2, brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 1-2)

**Defensible novelty claim.** The advance would be *multi-powder, feeder-first, uncertainty-quantified inverse calibration of effective contact parameters from a multivariate dosing fingerprint, prospectively validated against tests withheld from fitting and against measured recoated-layer quality*—not the first use of a screw feeder to calibrate DEM. The examined precedents do not establish that tilt response, solenoid-tap release, post-stop afterflow, and zero-flow increment frequency have jointly been used as inverse-calibration observables. In reporting results, distinguish an inferred, model- and wall-material-dependent **effective** friction/cohesion parameter from an independently measured intrinsic powder property; likewise, moisture sensitivity requires controlled moisture variation, and a claim about spreadability requires an actual spreading measurement rather than funnel flow alone. The observed failure of consolidation-calibrated parameters to transfer to spreading makes that last independent test especially consequential. (imole2016reprintof"experiments pages 1-5, shen2021calibrationofdiscrete pages 1-2, kassem2021asemiautomateddem pages 12-13, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 11-14, brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 1-2)

info.query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. El Kassem et al. (KONA Powder and Particle Journal 38, 2021, 235-250, doi:10.14356/kona.2021010) calibrated DEM contact parameters of one free-flowing lactose powder from the angle of repose, bulk density and mass flow rate measured with an auger dosing device, using a design of experiments and regression. Beyond that paper and its direct predecessors by the same group: has anyone used the measured response of a screw or auger doser or feeder (mass per revolution or flow rate versus screw speed, tilt angle or fill level, flow intermittency, afterflow) as the primary data to infer DEM or continuum contact parameters for several different powders, with uncertainty quantification such as Bayesian calibration, and then checked the inferred values against standard tests that were not used in the fit (shear cell, Hall or Carney flow, tapped density, spreading)?
